flashcard_questions.q: What is a sequence in music?
flashcard_questions.a: A pattern repeated immediately at a higher or lower pitch.
A short pattern that repeats continuously through a section or piece.
One part copies another closely, but not exactly, shortly after.
A sustained or repeated note, usually in the bass, under changing harmony.
Two sustained notes, usually tonic and dominant, held continuously beneath a melody.
Two or more parts play the same melody exactly, starting at different times.

flashcard_questions.q: How does canon differ from imitation?
flashcard_questions.a: In a canon the copy is exact; in imitation it is only close.
A pedal note placed in the highest part instead of the bass.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Vivaldi concerto uses ascending sequences to portray biting winds?
Which famous canon by Pachelbel is built over a repeating bass line?

flashcard_questions.a: A broken chord whose notes are played in order, low to high.

flashcard_questions.q: Which note pattern does an Alberti bass follow?

flashcard_questions.a: Balanced phrases of equal length, usually four or eight bars.
A short, memorable musical idea used as a building block.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Beethoven symphony is built on a four-note motif?

notes: 15 cards: 9 device term-to-definition cards (sequence, ostinato, imitation, pedal, inverted pedal, drone, canon, arpeggio, motif) plus regular phrasing, 1 misconception card separating canon from imitation, 1 pattern card (Alberti bass), and 3 example-to-feature cards on named works (Vivaldi's Winter, Pachelbel's Canon in D, Beethoven's Fifth). Broken chord was dropped because the arpeggio card already carries it, and the era table was dropped as it only yields list answers.
